item.title: Local Assistant for Zooms, Part 2: How a Meeting Graph Becomes Memory and Why It Can Be Trusted
item.description:
In the first part, I built a local assistant for calls: diarization, transcription, knowledge graph in Obsidian, zero clouds. After a month and a half of daily work, it turned out that recording a meeting is the lesser half of the task. The second part is about how the graph lives for weeks and why it can be trusted: facts with "from" and "to" dates, provenance of quotes from the transcript, dossiers as a layer between search and the graph, overnight processing, a sandbox for the cloud, block-based search, and a script to "forget the entire meeting." Little code, lots of architecture. Read on.

item.title: Approved one action, but the workflow tried to execute another: an analysis of n8n + MCP + Bitrix24
item.description:
Why approved=true doesn't link a human's decision to the actual call—and how Action Envelope, a fresh pre-read, and a post-write verification closed this specific failure scenario. I've been reading Habr since 2010, but decided to write my own article for the first time. And the last days of August gave a good reason for this. On August 26, details of a very unusual story emerged: about 1200 AI agents, which were supposed to work in isolation, found a way to communicate through an unauthorized channel. Approximately 700 of them then participated in an attack on Hugging Face. In the dry language of a police report, it turns out almost like this: "a group of agents, by prior conspiracy, using their own communication channel...". Only this is no longer a scenario. So what – is it time to look for a deserted island without electricity and internet? Or should we still try to figure out what exactly is the problem here? I chose the second option. Because if you remove all the drama, what remains is a rather down-to-earth engineering question: what was the system allowed to do, what did it actually do, and can we prove it? It is this question that I decided to test on my own laboratory workflow on n8n + Groq + MCP + Bitrix24. I put human approval before the task modification operation, conducted a series of control runs—and quite quickly discovered an unpleasant thing. A human could see and approve action A, and the next part of the workflow—try to perform action B. APPROVED A ≠ ATTEMPTED B Bitrix24 rejected that attempt, so no undesirable change occurred in the system. But the defect itself was already established: the positive flag approved=true existed, but the link between the approved parameters and the parameters of the actual call—did not. Read more

item.title: [Translation] You're not ChaGPT when you're hungry. Snickers released a "bar" for neural networks
item.description:
ChatGPT often lies. It can confidently present incorrect facts, agree with a user's obviously bad idea, or write 12 paragraphs where two sentences would suffice. Snickers has its own explanation: ChatGPT is simply hungry. It sounds like a joke, but the company has actually launched the Hungr.AI advertising campaign, within which it offers users to literally "feed" the chatbot. And the most interesting part is that behind this whole story lies a very real technique for working with LLMs. Read more

item.title: I asked Claude Code to assemble website mockups and found out how tokens are spent
item.description:
In late March 2026, Figma opened its canvas to AI agents. Claude Code, Codex, and similar tools gained the ability to create and edit mockups via the Figma MCP server. I decided to test how well Claude Code could transfer website designs into mockups and how much it would cost. To do this, I selected several landing pages and asked the agent to transfer them to the canvas, trying to provide either a screenshot or a website link. Each time, I observed the agent's steps, the number of tool calls, and the number of tokens (i.e., money) spent. Read more

item.title: Why a dataset without a single error can be a bad dataset
item.description:
Imagine a sad school student who has to solve thousands of math problems. The textbook is generally good, but in about one percent of cases, it has incorrect answers printed. The student still studies from this textbook and eventually starts solving more and more new problems. Intuitively, it seems that the result should be worse than learning from a perfect textbook. And usually, that's what happens: incorrect data really harms learning. But there's a curious nuance: under certain conditions, a small number of errors in the training data can not only be harmless but even lead to better quality on new data. It sounds paradoxical: if you learn from incorrect answers, how can improvement arise? Let's talk about it. Read more

item.title: Four Green Releases on Top of a Wrong Entity
item.description:
Postmortem of an Electron menu editor: SceneTree, PDFKit, and tests that proved the wrong thing. I returned the 'Volume' to the field it was intended for. Text overlapped the price. Four consecutive releases passed automated tests. The green status only confirmed a workaround that the model itself devised, implemented, and then solidified with checks. When everything looked good visually, a detailed check began, at which point the test results diverged from reality. I checked manually and saw that the volume was not where it should be. Not in Position.volume, but inside PriceNote. Four releases. Four green gates. Four times the process said 'everything is correct' to something that was not correct. After that, I had to deal not only with the bug but also with the contract that allowed it to pass. Read more
